newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish drivers continue strike, disruption spreads.
newsitem.headline: Danish drivers continue strike, disruption spreads.

text.p: Militant Danish truckers voted Thursday to continue a four-day blockade of seaports and frontier crossings in a dispute which has already seriously disrupted the country's foreign trade.
"We have chosen to continue our action for the time being," drivers' spokesman Ole Prusse told Reuters from protest headquarters at the Padborg border crossing to Germany.

"We have sent a couple of our people to parliament in Copenhagen to explain our case. I would stress that this is not a negotiating team, we just want to make our situation clear to the politicians," he added.
The protest, against government plans to cut drivers' overseas subsistence allowances, was not related to nationwide protests by French truckers.
Tax Minister Carsten Koch Wednesday offered to shelve cuts and raise the current 150 crown ($25.50) daily allowance to 250 crowns ($42.50) but the drivers insist on at least 500 crowns ($85).
Prusse said the truckers would meet later Thursday in Padborg to reassess the situation and mull possible new moves.

Some 2,000 Danish drivers have stopped goods traffic from crossing the land border with Germany since Monday, and have since broadened the blockade to most ports, halting exports to Norway, Sweden, Germany, Britain and eastern European countries.
Police said that around 2,000 trucks on Thursday still blocked freight from entering or leaving Denmark at Padborg, but that private cars were being allowed through.
The Danish hauliers' action, combined with the truckers' strike in France has clogged highways and ports and disrupted industry and commerce throughout much of Europe.
Swedish vehicle makers Volvo and Saab said that they might have to cut production next week if road haulage chaos continued.

On Wednesday German car manufacturer Volkswagen said the strikes were disrupting production and German airline Lufthansa put larger planes on its daily Copenhagen-Frankfurt cargo flight in an effort to partially make up for lost road freight.

The port blockades hurt not only international trade but also domestic shipments between the main production centres of the Jutland peninsula and Denmark's islands, particularly Zealand where the capital, Copenhagen is located.

Supermarket chains on the island, where about half Denmark's five million people live, warned of food shortages next week affecting dairy products, meat and bread in particular if ports remained closed.
